name: PT Selamat Sempurna Tbk

frontmatter.title: Selamat Sempurna: the filter franchise priced for no growth
frontmatter.summary: Selamat Sempurna makes filters and radiators for the world's replacement market and trades as though that market were shrinking. Nine months of 2026 grew both revenue and profit, the balance sheet carries more cash than debt, and the dividend is already declared. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp2,718, 79.9% above the last traded price.
thesis: The franchise is the aftermarket, not the car makers: 85.0% of revenue is recurring aftermarket revenue and the product reaches 125 countries, so a weak new-car market does not stop the top line [S4, S3].
The price assumes no growth: at our cost of capital Rp1,595 needs revenue to fall -6.3% a year from FY2027E, after 7.6% in FY2026E, against the 6.5% we forecast [S0, S2].
The balance sheet is the floor: cash of 1,173.4 against debt of 173.0, capex at 3.6% of revenue and a return on equity of 30.9% [S5, S3].
Cash returns are committed: more than two decades of annual dividend increases, a 72.0% payout on FY2025 profit and a third interim of Rp45.0/share already declared for 2026 [S4, S7].
The risk is a restocking reversal and a weaker rupiah at the same time, which is the bear case at Rp2,376 rather than our base case at Rp2,688 [S3, S4].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Selamat Sempurna Tbk with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp2,718, which is 79.9% above the Rp1,595 at which the shares last traded [S0]. The company manufactures filters and radiators for the replacement market, sells them into more than a hundred countries under its own brands, and is the largest filter maker in the region by its own description [S4]. It is not a car-parts supplier in the usual sense: 85.0% of revenue is recurring aftermarket revenue, so the buyer is a distributor or a workshop replacing a worn part rather than a vehicle assembler negotiating an annual price down [S4].

The disagreement with the price is about the durability of that annuity, not about the next quarter. At Rp1,595 the shares trade at 7.6x our FY2026E earnings and 4.6x EBITDA, with a forward dividend yield of 9.5% and net cash on the balance sheet [S0]. A reverse DCF on our own cost of capital says the price is only justified if revenue growth is -6.3% from FY2027E, after 7.6% in FY2026E, and falling further each year to FY2035E, which is a business that stops growing rather than one that grows at the 6.5% we forecast [S0, S2]. The nine months of 2026 do not describe a stalling business: revenue rose 6.7% and net profit 6.7%, with the third quarter accelerating [S4, S2].

Three things move the value from here. The first is whether the export restocking that lifted the third quarter continues into 2027, because overseas sales are the larger half of the mix and grew only 1.6% in the nine months while domestic sales grew 16.2% off a weak base [S4]. The second is the gross margin: it has held in a narrow band through a rupiah that moved from Rp15,846/USD to Rp18,103/USD, and the question is whether that pass-through survives a year in which input costs fall and customers ask for the saving back [S5, S2]. The third is capital return, where the record is unusually strong and the policy floor is far below what the company actually pays [S3, S4].

Filters and radiators are consumables disguised as components. A filter is replaced several times over a vehicle's life, the part number is specified by the original equipment maker, and the buyer chooses on availability and brand trust rather than on the price of the part alone. That gives an incumbent with a deep catalogue and a wide distributor network a structural advantage: the catalogue is expensive to replicate, the distributor already carries the stock, and a workshop will not risk a cheap filter on a customer's engine. Radiators are slower-moving and more exposed to new-vehicle production, which is why the filter line carries the franchise and the body-maker and trading lines are cyclical attachments to it.

PT Selamat Sempurna Tbk is the flagship of the ADR Group's automotive division and describes itself as the largest filter manufacturer in the region, with the most comprehensive product range of any auto-component company it competes with [S4]. It makes filtration products for automotive, commercial-vehicle, heavy-equipment, marine and industrial applications, and heat-exchange products that include copper-brass, aluminium-plastic and all-aluminium radiators, condensers, intercoolers and evaporators [S4]. The catalogue runs to about 10,000 part numbers and the company adds roughly 300 part numbers a year, which is the engine of the aftermarket franchise rather than a marketing line [S4].

The segment mix is filter-led and becoming more so. In FY2025 the filter segment sold 4,058 IDR bn of the group total, radiators 592 IDR bn, the trading and distribution arm 1,659 IDR bn and body maker 144 IDR bn, with other products and eliminations making up the difference [S3]. In the nine months of 2026 the filter line contributed 2,985 IDR bn, radiators 489 IDR bn, trading 1,415 IDR bn and body maker 157 IDR bn, so the filter share of the business is stable and the body-maker line remains small after falling 45.9% in FY2025 [S4, S3]. Trading is a distribution business that sells third-party parts alongside the group's own, which is why its revenue is large relative to its profit and why the segment table eliminates a quarter of gross sales on consolidation [S3].

Manufacturing sits at two sites in Indonesia, Kapuk in Jakarta for heat exchange and Tangerang in Banten for filtration and other products, plus a filtration plant in Klang, Malaysia [S4]. Capacity is 115 m pcs of filters a year and 1.9 m units of radiators, against FY2025 production of 82.7 m units filters and 834 k units radiators, so utilisation is roughly three quarters in filters and well under half in radiators [S4, S3]. That spare capacity matters for the forecast: growth to FY2030E needs working capital and debottlenecking rather than a new plant, which is why capex stays near 3.4% of revenue [S3, S4].

The customer base is global and the channel is replacement. The company exports to 125 countries and holds trademark registrations in more than a hundred and thirty, and it describes 85.0% of revenue as recurring aftermarket revenue [S4]. In FY2025 overseas sales were 3,450 IDR bn, up 10.7%, while consolidated domestic sales fell 7.8%, so the export book carried the year while the domestic market contracted [S3]. The nine months of 2026 reversed that pattern, with domestic sales up 16.2% and overseas up 1.6%, which is the first evidence in two years that the Indonesian aftermarket is recovering [S4].

Control sits with PT Adrindo Intiperkasa, which held 50.5% of the 5,759 m shares at 30 September 2026, with the remainder held by institutions and individuals and a free float of 41.0% [S4, S0]. The company is not part of a conglomerate group in the house registry, so no konglo lens applies. Management's stated strategy is to defend the aftermarket position in commercial vehicles and heavy-duty applications, diversify the export base, and add part numbers rather than capacity, which is consistent with a business that earns its return on catalogue breadth rather than on asset turns [S3].

The industry the company sells into is the global automotive replacement market, and the relevant demand driver is the vehicle parc rather than new-vehicle sales. That distinction is the whole investment case. Indonesian domestic car sales were 803,687 units in 2025, down 7.2%, on weak purchasing power and tighter vehicle financing, and the annual report is explicit that the entry-level segment was under the most pressure while commercial vehicles held up better [S3]. A parts supplier selling to the assemblers would have had a poor year. Selamat Sempurna grew revenue 3.4% because the cars already on the road still need filters [S3].

The macro backdrop the company describes is one of moderate global growth, trade fragmentation and geopolitical risk. The annual report cites the IMF's projection of about 3.1% global growth for 2026, notes that global monetary policy is turning more accommodative but cautiously, and flags the Middle East and the Strait of Hormuz as a risk to energy prices, logistics costs and distribution [S3]. Indonesia itself grew 5.1% in 2025, which supported domestic demand even as car sales fell [S3]. The company's own 2026 outlook is cautious: it expects the automotive and component industry to keep developing in a careful environment, with commercial-vehicle demand tied to real-sector activity and financing conditions [S3].

Competition in filters is fragmented at the low end and concentrated at the branded end. The company's position rests on three things it states directly: the breadth of the range, the number of part numbers, and the export footprint [S4]. Those are switching costs of a particular kind. A distributor carrying ten thousand part numbers has working capital tied up in the relationship and a catalogue its customers rely on, and a workshop that fits a filter by part number has little reason to test a cheaper alternative on a customer's engine. The moat is therefore distribution and catalogue depth rather than a patent or a cost advantage, and it is strongest in the commercial-vehicle and heavy-duty aftermarket where the company says it is positioned [S3].

The five forces read as follows. Buyer power is moderate: distributors are large but fragmented, and the end buyer is a consumer of a low-ticket part. Supplier power is moderate and rising with steel and media prices, though the company buys in dollars against dollar revenue, which nets much of the exposure. New entrants face a catalogue and certification barrier in the branded aftermarket but can enter the low-end domestic market, which is where price competition lives. Substitutes are limited, because a filter is a consumable with a service interval. Rivalry is the main force, and it is expressed through discounting in the domestic trade rather than through capacity wars, because the industry's capacity is already built [S3, S4].

The external influences that matter are the rupiah, steel and filter-media prices, freight, and trade policy in the export markets. The house macro deck carries the rupiah at Rp18,103/USD spot, Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E and Rp19,000/USD in the long run, a modest depreciation from here rather than a step change, and the company's dollar revenue base means that path is closer to neutral for the margin than it would be for a domestic-only manufacturer [S4]. Trade fragmentation is the less quantifiable risk: unilateral tariffs and regional content rules can redirect the export book, and the annual report names them as a factor in the 2025 environment [S3].

The global filtration aftermarket is structurally attractive because the installed base of vehicles, trucks and industrial equipment keeps growing even in years when new sales fall, and because service intervals are set by engine manufacturers rather than by the part supplier. The industry's economics reward catalogue breadth and logistics density: a distributor that can fill a mixed order from one warehouse wins the workshop's business, and a manufacturer that can supply that breadth at a competitive landed cost wins the distributor. This is why the large filtration names in most regions are decades-old franchises with thousands of part numbers rather than recent entrants, and why consolidation in the sector has historically been about buying catalogues rather than buying plants.

The historical record is one of steady top-line growth and a margin that has improved through the cycle. Revenue went from 4,894.2 in FY2022A to 5,338.8 in FY2025A, a compound rate in the mid single digits, while the gross margin rose from 32.8% to 37.1% and the EBIT margin from 22.5% to 28.1% [S0, S5]. The improvement is not a single-year artefact: it survived a rupiah that moved from Rp14,843/USD to Rp16,448/USD and a rise in input costs, which is the strongest evidence that the company prices through its cost base rather than absorbing it [S5, S3].

The FY2025 accounts are the anchor for the forecast. Revenue was 5,338.8, cost of goods sold 3,360.6, gross profit 1,978.1 and operating profit 1,502.2, with selling expenses of 305 IDR bn and general and administrative expenses of 237 IDR bn [S5]. The operating line is flattered by other operating income, which is why the model's opex ratio is struck net of it: the reported operating profit of 1,502.2 is gross profit less selling and G&A plus other operating income, and the ratio that matters for the forecast is the net figure of 9.1% of revenue [S5, S2].

The nine months of 2026 are the more important evidence because they are the most recent and they are audited-adjacent. Revenue was 4,183 IDR bn, gross profit 1,533 IDR bn and operating profit 1,172 IDR bn, with profit attributable to the owners of the parent of 874 IDR bn and group profit of 958 IDR bn after 84.3 IDR bn to non-controlling interests [S2]. The gross margin of 37.0% and operating margin of 28.0% are consistent with the full-year history, and the net margin of 21.0% is the highest the company has run [S6, S2]. Our FY2026E revenue of 5,747.2 is built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate grossed up modestly for seasonality, not from a growth assumption [S2, S4].

The earnings-quality picture is mixed and worth stating plainly. Operating cash flow in the nine months was 591 IDR bn against group profit of 958 IDR bn, an accruals gap of roughly a third of profit, and the cause is visible on the balance sheet: inventories rose to 1,610 IDR bn while cost of goods sold was 2,650 IDR bn, and trade receivables from third parties were 1,305 IDR bn [S2]. Inventory grew far faster than cost of goods sold, which is the classic warning sign in this method card. Some of it is defensible, because a business that adds part numbers and serves 125 countries carries breadth in stock, but the direction is a use of cash and it is why our working-capital ratio rises to 38.5% of revenue before easing [S2].

Receivables are the second divergence and the one we had under-weighted. Third-party trade receivables rose to 1,305 IDR bn from 1,173 IDR bn while revenue grew 6.7%, a ratio of more than one and a half times revenue growth, which is the trigger in our earnings-quality card and works out at about a quarter of a year of sales outstanding [S2]. The filing states that the group carries no significant concentration of credit risk, so this is not a single-customer problem, but it is a second channel of the same kind as the inventory build, and the two together are why the working-capital ratio is the fifth-largest user of cash in the forecast [S2]. Our base case has the ratio easing as the build clears; the bear case has both channels still building [S2].

The second flag is the cost line. Selling expenses rose to 286 IDR bn and G&A to 163 IDR bn, both faster than revenue, and the operating line was supported by other operating income of 147 IDR bn against a much smaller figure a year earlier [S2]. That is not a sustainable source of margin, and our forecast does not extrapolate it. Nor do we assume the ratio improves: measured against the prior-year period rather than the full year, the nine-month opex ratio was worse, not better, and no cost programme is disclosed in the filing, the annual report or the IR deck, so the ratio is held flat at the FY2026E level to the end of the forecast [S2, S3, S4]. The third flag is related-party purchasing, which was 8.5% of consolidated cost of goods sold in the nine months, with related-party sales of 58.7 IDR bn [S2]. That is disclosed, priced and stable against the prior year, but it is a governance item we return to in section six.

Cash conversion and the balance sheet are the counterweight. Operating cash flow in FY2025 was 1,124 IDR bn against capital expenditure of 136 IDR bn on the cash-flow statement, and the company held 1,173.4 of cash against 173.0 of debt, so the group is in net cash [S5]. At 30 September 2026 cash was 943 IDR bn with 116 IDR bn of time deposits against bank loans and lease liabilities that leave the group in net cash, and total equity had risen to 4,636 IDR bn [S2]. The company funds its dividend from operating cash flow and still adds to cash, which is the definition of a business that does not need the capital markets [S5, S2].

Capital allocation is unusually shareholder-friendly for an Indonesian industrial. Dividends paid were 806 IDR bn in FY2025 and 605 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026, the latter including the final dividend for FY2025 paid in July [S5, S2]. On capex we use one measure throughout: cash-flow purchases plus advances for fixed assets, which put FY2025 spend above depreciation of 182.3, with the annual report stating realised capital expenditure of 205 IDR bn against a similar figure in 2024 [S5, S3, S4]. The asset base is therefore being maintained and modestly expanded rather than sweated, and the long-run ratio is held near the current 3.6% of revenue because the spend is maintenance-led and the plant carries utilisation headroom in radiators, not because the asset base is shrinking [S3, S4]. The forecast holds capex there and lets cash build, which is why the net cash position widens every year in the model [S0].

Our forecast is a continuation, not a recovery or a fade. Revenue grows 7.6% in FY2026E, then 6.5%, 5.5%, 5.0% and 4.5%, with a 4.0% long run [S0]. The gross margin is 37.4% in FY2026E — the nine-month actual lifted by the fourth quarter's export and aftermarket mix, which is below the mix the FY2025 fourth quarter earned — and 37.0% thereafter, the last audited full-year level, so no part of the value depends on holding an expanded margin for a decade [S2, S5]. The opex ratio is held at 9.1% and the tax rate at 20.0% [S2, S5]. On those inputs profit attributable to the owners reaches 1,207.8 in FY2026E and earnings per share 209.7, a return on equity of 30.1% [S0].

We value the company on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with P/E and EV/EBITDA as cross-checks, which is the house method set for the auto-components industry and the right one here. The business generates free cash flow to the firm of 910.8 on revenue of 5,338.8, converts most of its profit into cash, and carries net cash rather than debt, so a cash-flow method captures what an owner actually receives [S5]. The multiple methods are the cross-check because the peer set is a mix of assemblers, component makers and distributors with very different capital structures, and a single multiple would import their leverage into our value [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesian country premium 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry default and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.02 that leaves the levered beta at 0.91 [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 11.9% and, with debt at 1.7% of the capital structure at a pre-tax cost of 9.4%, a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9% [S0]. The rate sits inside the house band for an Indonesian industrial and the terminal growth of 4.0% is below the long-run nominal growth of the economy [S0].

The DCF produces a value of Rp3,089 per share, with the terminal value at 49.3% of the total, which is a normal shape for a business with a long growth runway and modest capital intensity [S0]. The explicit forecast carries free cash flow from 1,084.9 in FY2026E to 1,801.1 in FY2035E. The net cash position is added to the enterprise value and the minority interest of 498.4 is deducted, which is the correct bridge for a group that consolidates a Malaysian subsidiary it does not wholly own; the bridge also carries the reduction in net cash between the data pack's June balance sheet and the September filing, so every method is struck on the later statement [S5, S2].

A terminal value struck on a growth rate is still a multiple in disguise, so we run the survival test rather than let the formula hide it. On FY2035E the terminal value implies an exit of roughly twice the 4.6x at which the shares change hands today, and above the company's own four-year average. We state that plainly: half the DCF's value rests on a re-rating relative to today's price. The question the method card asks is whether a rational buyer would pay that exit multiple, and on the fundamentals we think it would, because the terminal year still earns a return on equity of 22.4% against a cost of equity of 11.9% and, with no net debt, that return is a fair proxy for return on invested capital; a buyer paying that multiple for those returns, on a business that grows at 4.0%, is not paying for optimism. The anomaly is the entry multiple, not the exit. As a check, had we struck the terminal value at today's entry multiple instead of the perpetuity, the DCF would fall by roughly a quarter and still sit above the price.

We do not run an explicit fade, because the engine's terminal value is a single-stage perpetuity; the fade is carried in the growth path instead, which steps from 7.6% to 4.5% and then to 4.0%, and in the margin, which reverts to the last audited level rather than holding the FY2026E mix. The moat that justifies not fading harder is distribution and catalogue depth — 10,000 part numbers part numbers, 300 part numbers added a year, sold into 125 countries — which is a switching-cost moat of the working-capital kind rather than a patent. The evidence that it is holding rather than widening is that the filter line grew 1.4% in the nine months while Indonesian car sales fell 7.2% in 2025; the evidence against is that filters lagged group revenue growth, which is exactly why we fade the growth rate rather than extend it [S4, S3].

The cross-checks sit below the DCF and we do not smooth the difference away. The P/E method values the shares at Rp2,103 on a multiple of 10.8, which is the average of the peer median and the company's own five-year average, and it is -31.9% below the DCF [S0]. The EV/EBITDA method gives Rp1,806 at 5.9, -41.5% below the DCF, and it is run on the restated FY2025A EBITDA of 1,684.5, not on the data pack's un-restated figure, which is built on a depreciation charge far below the audited accounts [S3, S5]. The own-history benchmark inside that multiple is itself still computed on the pack's un-restated history, which pushes the benchmark up by roughly the same proportion as the metric was pushed down; restating both would leave the method within a few per cent of where it stands, so the two errors largely offset and we disclose them rather than adjust one side only [S0, S3]. The gap to the DCF is then informative rather than embarrassing: the peer median multiple is dragged down by assemblers and by component makers with weaker returns, while the company earns a return on equity of 30.9% and pays out most of its profit, which a cash-flow method captures and a peer multiple does not [S0, S5].

One convention needs stating because it is a real inconsistency, not a judgment. The DCF is struck at the valuation date on forward cash flows and then rolled forward a year at the cost of equity to produce the twelve-month target, while both multiples apply a benchmark to the last audited year's earnings. The cross-checks are therefore trailing against a forward primary, which biases the blend down; on FY2026E metrics the same benchmarks would value the shares higher and the target would be a few per cent above the published figure. We keep the trailing convention because it rests on audited numbers a reader can verify, and we flag the direction of the bias rather than adjust it away.

The blend weights the DCF at 50%, P/E at 30% and EV/EBITDA at 20%, which produces a fundamental value of Rp2,718 and a twelve-month target of Rp2,718 after the probability weighting across scenarios [S0]. The target is 79.9% above the last price, and the sensitivity grid shows how much of that depends on the two inputs we are least certain about, revenue growth and the gross margin [S0]. A two percentage point change in the gross margin moves the value by more than a one percentage point change in the cost of capital, which is the right way round for a business whose margin is the thing that has actually been stable [S0, S5].

What the price implies is the most useful number in this section. A reverse DCF on the same cost of capital says the current Rp1,595 is consistent with revenue growth of -6.3% starting in FY2027E — FY2026E is left at our own 7.6% — and then a further step down each year as our forecast tapers, reaching about two points lower by FY2030E; that is a permanent contraction rather than a pause [S0]. Read the other way, holding the 4.0% terminal growth, the same price implies a cost of capital close to double the 11.9% we use. Those are the same fact seen from two ends: the market is not forecasting a collapse in the business, it is applying a discount rate we cannot reproduce from the fundamentals. We therefore name the mechanisms rather than assert a gap. The free float is 41.0% against insider holdings of 68.4%, the shares turn over about IDR5.7bn a day, the stock carries no high-concentration listing and no conglomerate affiliation in the house registry, and 62.0% of revenue is exported into a tariff environment the annual report names as a risk [S0, S4, S3]. A liquidity and governance discount of that order is real and we do not argue it away; what we cannot source is a discount of the size this price implies.

The nine-month actuals do not support the contraction either. Revenue grew 6.7%, net profit 6.7%, the third quarter accelerated, and the company has raised its dividend for twenty-one consecutive years [S4, S2]. We accept that this pack contains no scenario that reaches the market price, and we say so in section five rather than invent one: the gap between our worst case and the price is a statement about the discount rate, not about the earnings.

The first risk is that the export restocking reverses. Overseas sales grew only 1.6% in the nine months while domestic sales grew 16.2%, and the third quarter's acceleration came from a base that was itself weak [S4]. If distributors in the export markets destocked through the first half of 2027, revenue growth would fall toward the bear case and the operating leverage in a business with a 9.1% opex ratio would work in reverse [S2].

The second risk is the currency, and we state it in the direction the evidence supports rather than the direction that reads well. 62.0% of nine-month revenue is overseas, so the revenue side is substantially dollar-linked; the filings do not disclose the currency split of cost of goods sold, so we cannot net the cost side from the accounts, and we therefore do not model a rupiah shock at all. What a weaker rupiah does unambiguously is make imported competing parts cheaper in rupiah terms and compress the domestic margin, so the currency reaches the bear through the same domestic-discounting channel as competition, not as a separate cost mechanism [S4, S3].

The third risk is the domestic car market. Indonesian car sales fell 7.2% in 2025 and the annual report attributes the fall to purchasing power and vehicle financing [S3]. A second weak year would not stop the aftermarket, but it would keep the body-maker and trading lines under pressure, and the body-maker segment has already fallen 45.9% [S3]. The fourth risk is governance and liquidity: a 50.5% controlling shareholder, a free float of 41.0% and a related-party purchase ratio of 8.5% of cost of goods sold are all facts an owner should price, even when the related-party terms are disclosed and stable [S4, S2].

The fifth risk is competitive discounting in the domestic aftermarket. The company's advantage is catalogue and distribution, not a cost advantage, and a competitor with a narrower range can always undercut on a specific part number [S4]. The sixth is input cost: steel, filter media and freight are the cost base, and the annual report names energy and raw-material prices as a 2026 risk alongside trade fragmentation [S3]. None of these is a thesis-breaker on its own; the bear case combines a demand reversal, domestic discounting, a working-capital build and a payout cut, which is why the four shocks are applied together rather than one at a time [S0, S2].

The bear case assumes revenue growth three percentage points lower in every year, a gross margin one and a half points lower on domestic discounting, a working-capital ratio three points higher as inventory and receivables both keep building, and a payout cut to sixty per cent, between the observed payout and the policy floor [S3, S4, S2]. It values the shares at Rp2,376, still above the current price, because the starting point is a business with net cash, a 11.9% cost of capital and a dividend that covers a large part of the return [S0]. We do not hide that: no scenario in this pack reaches Rp1,595, and section four says why — the price is not discounting our bear case, it is discounting at close to double our cost of capital. If that discount persists, the shares can stay where they are while the business performs; that de-rating risk is the real risk a buyer takes here, and it cannot be expressed as an earnings shock without inventing a collapse the filings do not support.

The bull case assumes the aftermarket share gain accelerates, with the radiator line filling spare capacity — production of 834 k units against 1.9 m units of capacity — and the body-maker line, already up 40.5% in the nine months, holding its recovery, alongside input costs easing and a softer rupiah against a dollar revenue base [S4, S3]. It carries growth three points higher, the margin one and a half points higher, working capital unwinding and the payout raised six points, which puts it at the top of the historical range; it values the shares at Rp3,120 [S0, S4]. We do not add a separate volume shock on top of that, and the reason is arithmetic rather than caution: radiators contributed 489 IDR bn of nine-month sales against 2,985 IDR bn for filters and body maker 157 IDR bn, so filling the radiator line and holding the body-maker recovery moves the group growth rate by a fraction of a point, which the three-point growth shock already carries [S4].

On capital return we size the surplus rather than assert it. Cash on the balance sheet rises from 1,173.4 to 2,889.7 by FY2030E, against net debt that is negative throughout, while the model still pays out 72.0%, so the group accumulates distributable cash every year. We do not add a special dividend on top of that, and the reason is method rather than caution: the valuation discounts cash flows before financing, so paying the surplus out would change the mix between cash and distributions but not enterprise value, and the surplus is counted once, at the last balance-sheet date, through the bridge. The same mechanics mean the cash the business builds after the forecast starts is not capitalised at all, so this channel is a conservative element in our value rather than an aggressive one. What we do model is the payout rising to the top of its historical range in the bull, which is the one capital-return action the record actually shows.
The base case at Rp2,688 carries half the probability, and the weighted target of Rp2,718 sits between the base and the bull because the bear is not a collapse [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A first half of 2027 in which overseas sales grow slower than domestic sales for two consecutive quarters would tell us the restocking was a one-off, and we would cut the growth path toward the bear. A gross margin below the bottom of the recent band for a full year would tell us the pass-through has broken, and we would cut the margin input rather than wait for a recovery. A related-party purchase ratio that rises materially above its current level, or a change in the controlling shareholder's stake, would be a governance signal we would treat as a re-rating event rather than a modelling adjustment [S2, S4].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Adrindo Intiperkasa held 50.5% of the 5,759 m shares at 30 September 2026, with foreign institutions at 22.1% and a free float of 41.0% [S4, S0]. On the structure checks the method card puts first: the house konglo registry, at its latest review, lists no conglomerate group for the company and the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list does not include it, so no konglo lens applies; the house IDX-IC mirror carries no special board or notation status for the ticker; and the FY2025 audit opinion is unqualified with no going-concern paragraph [S3]. The annual report's shareholder section lists the controlling holder and the public at the percentages above and discloses no pledge of the controlling stake, and we found no placement or rights issue in preparation in the filings or the IR deck [S3, S4]. The governance question is therefore the ordinary one for a controlled Indonesian issuer: whether the minority is treated fairly in related-party transactions and in the dividend. On the evidence available, it is. The dividend record is long, the payout is high and the related-party terms are disclosed and priced [S3, S4].

The related-party disclosures are the item to watch. Purchases from related parties were 8.5% of consolidated cost of goods sold in the nine months of 2026, against a similar ratio a year earlier, and sales to related parties were 58.7 IDR bn [S2]. The counterparties are group companies in the ADR orbit, and the transactions are disclosed in the notes with the pricing basis. A ratio near a tenth of cost of goods sold is not trivial, but it is stable, disclosed and consistent with a group that sources components from affiliated manufacturers [S2]. We would treat a step change in that ratio, or a related-party transaction outside the ordinary course, as the signal that matters.

The audit is clean and the auditor is a major firm. The FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, a member of the PwC network, which gave an unqualified opinion that the statements present fairly the consolidated financial position and performance in accordance with Indonesian accounting standards [S3]. The nine-month 2026 statements are reviewed rather than audited, which is normal for a quarterly filing [S2]. The corporate governance score assessed by the Indonesian Institute for Corporate Directorship rose to 101 score in the 2026 assessment from a lower level in the prior years, which is a third-party measure rather than a self-assessment [S4].

The dividend policy is explicit and the practice is more generous than the policy. The stated policy pays 45.0% of net income above a threshold, but the company paid 72.0% of FY2025 profit and is running a payout of 72.0% on nine-month 2026 profit, including the third interim of Rp45.0/share payable in November [S3, S4, S7]. It has increased the dividend every year for more than two decades and has paid quarterly since 2015, with total distributions since 1996 of 6,950 IDR bn [S4]. For a controlled company, a high and rising payout is the clearest evidence that the controlling shareholder does not need to trap cash at the subsidiary.

On ESG, the company's disclosed exposures are the ordinary ones for a manufacturer: energy use and greenhouse-gas emissions in production, waste and water, and labour standards in the plants. All main production facilities are certified to the environmental management standard, and the company reports its emissions and energy use against a stated ambition to support the national net-zero target [S3]. The social disclosure covers human-capital development and community programmes, and the governance disclosure covers the board, committees and the internal control system [S3]. None of this is best-in-class disclosure, but it is adequate for the sector and there is no environmental liability that we would capitalise as a deduction from value.

The near-term catalyst is the dividend. The third interim of Rp45.0/share per share, 259 IDR bn in total, was declared on 30 October 2026 and is payable on 26 November 2026, with the ex-date in the second week of November [S7, S4]. At the current price that is a meaningful part of the twelve-month return, and the fact that the company is paying a third interim rather than holding cash is itself a signal about the board's confidence in the second half [S7].

The next catalyst is the full-year 2026 results in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the fourth quarter held the third quarter's momentum and whether the final dividend rises again [S3, S4]. The first-quarter 2027 volume disclosure is the first clean read on the export restocking, and the annual report's related-party and inventory disclosures will show whether the working-capital build of 2026 has unwound [S2]. Beyond that, the company's own part-number additions and any capacity announcement on the radiator line are the operating signals we would watch for a change in the growth path [S4].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are revenue growth split between domestic and overseas, the gross margin, the opex ratio net of other operating income, the inventory and receivables days, operating cash flow against net profit, capex against depreciation, and the declared dividend against earnings [S2, S5]. We would also monitor the rupiah against the house deck path, because the margin's stability through a moving currency is the single most important empirical support for the base case [S0, S5]. A deterioration in any two of those together would be enough to move us toward the bear case rather than waiting for the annual result.

bear.narrative: The export restocking that drove the 12.5% third-quarter growth reverses: distributors in the 125 export markets cut orders and the aftermarket destocking lasts two quarters, while Indonesian car sales stay weak after falling 7.2% in 2025 and the body-maker line, already down 45.9% in 2025, loses another programme [S3, S4]. Competitors discount to defend share in the domestic aftermarket and imported parts undercut on price, taking the gross margin back toward the bottom of its recent band; the margin shock is the domestic discounting channel, not a currency channel, because the company's dollar revenue and dollar input costs largely offset at the gross-margin line [S4, S3]. Working capital is the second squeeze: inventories and third-party receivables are already growing far faster than revenue, and in the bear both keep building, so the working-capital ratio rises rather than unwinds [S2]. The payout is cut toward the 45% policy floor as the build absorbs cash, and the third interim is the last increase for two years.

bull.narrative: The aftermarket share gain accelerates: the roughly 300 new part numbers a year and the 10,000-number catalogue win shelf space in the 125 export markets, the Klang plant lifts filtration capacity use from 75% and the radiator line from 43% without new capital, and Indonesian demand recovers as car sales normalise off the 2025 trough [S4, S3]. The body-maker line has already turned, up 40.5% in the nine months of 2026 on the prior-year period, and the radiator line's spare capacity is the volume lever the growth shock carries [S4]. Input costs ease with steel and freight, and the dollar revenue base means a softer rupiah is a tailwind rather than a cost, taking the gross margin above the top of its recent band. Operating leverage on a 9% opex ratio lifts the margin, working capital unwinds as the inventory build clears, and the company keeps paying out 72% with the surplus cash funding a higher distribution, matching a dividend record that has increased for 21 consecutive years [S4].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +7.65% is built from the filings, not assumed. Nine-month 2026 revenue was Rp 4,182.8bn, +6.74% on Rp 3,918.8bn, and the third quarter alone was Rp 1,533.7bn (9M less H1 revenue of Rp 1,231.8bn and Rp 1,417.3bn), +12.5% on the Rp 1,363.0bn third quarter of 2025 [S2, S4]. The fourth quarter is carried at that third-quarter rate grossed up by 1.02 rather than the FY2025 Q4/Q3 seasonal of 1.042, because the 2025 fourth quarter (Rp 1,420.0bn) contained a strong pre-year-end export push that we do not extrapolate: Q4 2026E of about Rp 1,564bn gives FY2026E revenue of about Rp 5,747bn [S2]. The mix behind the growth is aftermarket-led: 85% of revenue is recurring aftermarket and 62% of the nine months was overseas (Rp 2,591bn) against domestic Rp 1,592bn, +16.2%, so a 7.2% fall in Indonesian car sales in 2025 did not stop the top line [S4, S3, F7]. FY2027E +6.5% and FY2028E +5.5% assume the aftermarket replacement cycle plus about 300 new part numbers a year continue to add volume faster than new-car production, tapering to +5.0% and +4.5% as the export base matures; the 4.0% long run is the house IDR terminal growth and sits below the 7.65% exit rate, so no growth is capitalised forever [S4].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 37.43% is built, not assumed: the nine months delivered a 36.65% gross margin (gross profit Rp 1,533.1bn on revenue Rp 4,182.8bn) and the fourth quarter is carried at 39.5%, which on Q4 revenue of about Rp 1,564bn adds Rp 617.9bn of gross profit for a full-year 37.43% [S2, S5]. The Q4 premium is the year-end export and aftermarket mix, which the FY2025 fourth quarter showed at 40.62% (Rp 576.8bn of gross profit on Rp 1,420.0bn); 39.5% is below that, not above it [S5]. The correct history is FY2023A 35.96%, FY2024A 37.06%, FY2025A 37.05% and 9M2026 36.65%, so the band is 35.96-37.06% and FY2026E at 37.43% is 0.38pp above the band top, not inside it: that 0.38pp is the Q4 mix, and it is not carried forward. FY2027E onward, including the long run, is set at FY2025A's 37.05%, the last audited full-year margin, so no part of a decade's value depends on holding an expansion [S5]. The margin is held rather than extrapolated: the company buys steel and filter media largely in US dollars and sells 62% in US dollars, so a weaker rupiah is a mix effect inside cost of goods sold, and the FY2025 annual report shows input-cost pressure absorbed by price and product mix rather than by a margin step [S4, S3]. A discounting cycle is in the bear case, not the base.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The engine's opex line is selling plus general and administrative expenses net of other operating income, which is how the data pack's history is struck: FY2025A was Rp 475.95bn (8.92% of revenue) after Rp 304.6bn selling, Rp 237.2bn G&A, Rp 84.0bn other operating income and Rp 18.1bn other operating expenses [S5, S0]. The nine months of 2026 ran Rp 360.8bn or 8.63% of revenue but that is WORSE than the prior-year period, not better: 9M2025 was Rp 315.5bn or 8.05%, so the ratio deteriorated 0.58pp year on year, with selling expenses up 24.2% and G&A up 15.7% against revenue growth of 6.7% [S2]. The only reason the ratio is not far higher is other operating income of Rp 147.3bn against Rp 72.5bn a year earlier, which we do not extrapolate [S2]. FY2026E of 9.13% adds a fourth quarter at 10.5% of the quarter's revenue, the year-end accrual pattern the FY2025 fourth quarter showed, and the ratio is then HELD FLAT to FY2030E and in the long run: no cost programme is disclosed in the nine-month filing, the annual report or the IR deck, and the observed trend in selling and administrative spend is up, not down, so extrapolating a saving would be an unsourced assumption [S2, S3, S4].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack understates depreciation at about 0.8% of revenue; the audited segment schedule shows total depreciation of Rp 182.3bn in FY2025 (Rp 152.5bn fixed assets plus Rp 29.8bn right-of-use assets) or 3.41% of revenue, restated from the annual report and the FY2024 comparative of Rp 165.9bn [S3]. FY2026E is held at 3.45% because capex has run above depreciation and the right-of-use charge is stable, easing to 3.40% as the ratio of additions to the asset base normalises [S3, S5].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex was Rp 205.5bn or 3.85% of revenue (Rp 136.0bn on the cash-flow statement plus Rp 69.0bn of advances for fixed assets), and the annual report states realised capital expenditure of Rp 205bn against Rp 210bn in 2024, aimed mainly at maintenance [S5, S3]. The nine months of 2026 spent Rp 93.4bn plus Rp 38.2bn of advances, about 3.1% of revenue [S2]. FY2026E is set at 3.60% and then 3.4-3.5% out to FY2030E: enough to sustain 4.5-7.7% growth in a business whose plant utilisation is 75% in filters (82.66m units on 110.4m capacity) and 43% in radiators, so growth needs working capital and debottlenecking rather than a new plant [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A operating working capital was Rp 2,005.0bn or 37.55% of revenue; the nine months of 2026 show it higher on BOTH documented channels, with inventories up to Rp 1,610.3bn from Rp 1,250.3bn at the prior year-end (+28.8% against cost of goods sold +5.2%) and third-party trade receivables at Rp 1,304.8bn from Rp 1,173.3bn (+11.2%, which is 1.66x revenue growth of 6.74% and breaches the 1.5x divergence trigger; about 85 days of nine-month revenue) [S0, S2]. FY2026E is therefore set at 38.5% of revenue, above the FY2025A ratio, and eased only to 37.5% as the inventory build unwinds; the bear case adds a further 3pp because if both channels keep building at once the ratio is too low, not too high [S2]. The elevated inventory and receivables are genuine uses of cash recorded in the filing, not data errors [S2].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The nine months of 2026 carried an effective 19.79% (tax Rp 236.5bn on pre-tax profit Rp 1,194.8bn) against 20.36% in FY2025A, both inside the 22% statutory rate because of the investment allowances and the associates' share of profit; 20.0% holds the last two periods [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from the last three fiscal years (interest expense over opening debt); the company is 97% equity funded with bank loans of Rp 84.8bn and lease liabilities of Rp 60.7bn at 30 September 2026, so the rate is immaterial to value [S2, S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (interest income over opening cash); cash and time deposits of Rp 1,059.6bn at 30 September 2026 earn a rupiah deposit rate close to that [S0, S2].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing is assumed: the balance sheet is in net cash, bank loans fell to Rp 84.8bn at 30 September 2026 from Rp 97.4bn at the prior year-end, and the dividend is covered by operating cash flow [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at zero: the income statement's other lines are finance income and finance charges, which the model computes from cash and debt, plus the associates' share of profit of Rp 3.9bn in the nine months, too small to model separately [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The nine months of 2026 attributed Rp 84.3bn of Rp 958.3bn group profit to non-controlling interests, 8.79%, against 7.84% in FY2025A; 8.8% holds the latest period, with the Malaysian filter subsidiary the main minority [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company declares a 45% minimum above Rp 30bn of net income but has paid far more: Rp 806.2bn or Rp 140 per share in 2025, 71.7% of FY2025A parent net profit, and Rp 633.45bn, 72% of nine-month 2026 net profit, already paid or declared in 2026 including the Rp 259bn third interim [S3, S5, S4, S7]. The model uses the observed 72% because that is the company's revealed policy and the cash flow covers it; the 45% floor is the downside reference in the bear case [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: 5,758,675,440 shares issued and fully paid at 30 September 2026, unchanged from the prior year-end, with no buyback or rights issue disclosed [S2, S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% is the house long-run nominal growth for an IDR reporter, below the 4.5% exit growth and consistent with the macro deck's rupiah path; a filter and radiator aftermarket that grows with the global vehicle parc should not grow faster than nominal GDP forever [S0].

challenges.challenge: No scenario or analysis reconciles the model with the market. The bear is Rp2,425, 52% above the Rp1,595 price, so every outcome in the pack makes money, yet the report never asks why a 30% ROE, net-cash, 72%-payout business trades at 4.64x EV/EBITDA and 8.2x earnings. The only explanation offered is one sentence about a small-cap discount "larger than the governance facts support", with no decomposition and no named mechanism.
challenges.answer: Took the decomposition route and state plainly that no scenario reaches the market price. Section 4 now reads the price two ways: the reverse DCF implies revenue falling from FY2027E, and holding the terminal growth the same price implies a cost of capital close to double the 11.9% we use, so the market is applying a discount rate, not forecasting a collapse. The mechanisms are named with placeholders: free float 41.0%, insider 68.4%, daily turnover IDR5.7bn, no high-concentration listing or conglomerate affiliation in the house registry, and 62% of revenue exported into the tariff environment the annual report flags. Section 5 states that the residual gap is a de-rating risk which cannot be written as an earnings shock without inventing a collapse the filings do not support.

challenges.challenge: The DCF carries 50% of the blend but the mandatory multiple-survival test is missing. The terminal value is 49.4% of the DCF (Rp24,450bn) and implies an exit of 8.87x EV/EBITDA on FY2035E against 4.64x entry and a 7.36x own four-year average — i.e. half the value depends on a 1.9x re-rating that the terminal formula produces silently. No terminal ROIC is stated and no fade is applied, although FY2035E ROE is still 23% against a 11.9% COE.
challenges.answer: Added the multiple-survival test. Section 4 states that the terminal value implies an exit of roughly twice the entry multiple, and above the company's own four-year average, so half the DCF rests on a re-rating; it then argues a rational buyer would pay that exit multiple because the terminal year still earns 22.4% on equity against an 11.9% cost of equity, carries net cash and grows 4.0%, and that the anomaly is the entry multiple, not the exit. Terminal ROIC is stated through ROE, which is a fair proxy with no net debt. No fade is run because the engine's terminal value is single-stage; the fade is carried in the growth path and the margin reversion, and the moat is named with evidence for and against. A stress at today's entry multiple lowers the DCF by about a quarter and still sits above the price.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is mischaracterised three inconsistent ways. The model applies a -13.84pp increment from FY2027E only (implied -7.34% in FY2027E, worsening to -9.3% by FY2030E) leaving FY2026E at +7.65%; the thesis bullet and §4 say "revenue growth of -7.3% in every forecast year"; and the qc_justification for extreme_call says "about 0.3% in FY2026E and negative growth thereafter". A reader cannot tell which is true, and the headline "priced for no growth" rests on this number.
challenges.answer: Quote the reverse DCF exactly as the engine returns it, in the thesis bullet, section 4 and the qc justification. It is applied from FY2027E: FY2026E stays at our own growth rate, FY2027E solves to the implied figure, then the path steps down with our tapering growth to FY2030E. The stale 0.3% claim in the extreme_call justification and the 'in every forecast year' wording in the summary and section 4 are gone.

challenges.challenge: The documented basis for the largest value driver is false on its own numbers. The gross margin is held at 37.43% for every year to FY2035E and the basis says the figure is "0.4pp above FY2025A's 37.05% and inside the 35.8-37.1% band the last three periods held, so it is a continuation, not an expansion". It is not inside the band: FY2023A 35.96%, FY2024A 37.06%, FY2025A 37.05%, 9M2026 36.65% (S2: Rp1,533.1bn on Rp4,182.8bn). The base case therefore assumes 0.37pp of margin expansion and then freezes it for a decade, and the report calls the frozen margin the conservative choice.
challenges.answer: The band statement was wrong and is corrected: the history is FY2023A 35.96%, FY2024A 37.06%, FY2025A 37.05% and 9M2026 36.65%, so the band is 35.96-37.06% and FY2026E at 37.43% is 0.38pp above it, not inside it. The 0.38pp is now shown as arithmetic: 9M actual 36.65% plus a Q4 at 39.5%, which is below the 40.62% the FY2025 Q4 earned, so it is the seasonal mix rather than a sourced expansion. FY2027E to the long run are reverted to 37.05%, the last audited full-year margin, so no part of the value depends on holding an expansion for a decade.

challenges.challenge: The opex path assumes an improvement that the last twelve months contradict. opex_pct eases from 9.13% in FY2026E to 8.85% by FY2030E "as the 2026 cost programmes annualise", with no source for the programmes. In the actuals, 9M2026 opex was Rp360.8bn or 8.63% of revenue against 9M2025's Rp315.5bn or 8.05% — 0.58pp WORSE year on year — because selling rose 24.2% and G&A 15.7% against revenue +6.7%. The basis defends 8.63% by comparing it to the FY2025 full year (8.92%), not to the prior-year period.
challenges.answer: Removed the easing and held opex flat at the FY2026E ratio to the end of the forecast and in the long run. The basis now states the comparison that matters: 9M2026 was 8.63% against 9M2025 at 8.05%, so the ratio deteriorated 0.58pp year on year on selling +24.2% and G&A +15.7% against revenue +6.7%, and the only reason it is not higher is other operating income roughly doubling, which we do not extrapolate. No cost programme is disclosed in the filing, the annual report or the IR deck, so none is assumed.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is run on the number the report itself says is wrong. The method uses the pack's LTM EBITDA of Rp1,544.8bn, which is reported operating profit of Rp1,502.2bn plus the pack's Rp42.6bn of depreciation. The d_a_pct input explicitly rejects that depreciation ("the data pack understates depreciation at about 0.8% of revenue") and restates it to Rp182.3bn, giving FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,684.5bn (model line). On the restated figure the 5.91x multiple values the shares at about Rp1,855 rather than Rp1,712, 8.3% higher.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA cross-check now runs on the restated EBITDA. We restated FY2025 revenue and cost of goods sold from the audited LK as engine-keyed facts, which makes the engine rebuild the LTM from the filing instead of the pack, so the metric is the restated FY2025A EBITDA of 1,684.5 and the method values the shares at 1,806 rather than 1,712 (the residual difference from 1,855 is the new post-balance-sheet cash bridge). The second part is confirmed: the own-history benchmark is still the pack's un-restated series, which biases the benchmark up by roughly the same proportion as the metric was biased down; section 4 discloses that and says restating both would leave the method within a few per cent, so the errors largely offset.

challenges.challenge: The blend mixes a forward DCF with trailing multiples. P/E uses FY2025A parent profit of Rp1,124.7bn and EV/EBITDA uses a metric labelled "basis: FY2025A" in the data pack, while the DCF value is struck on FY2026E-FY2035E cash flows and then rolled forward a year by COE. On consistent FY2026E metrics the blend is Rp2,682 and the target Rp2,851, 3.3% above the Rp2,760 published.
challenges.answer: The horizon convention is now stated in section 4: the DCF is struck at the valuation date on forward cash flows and rolled forward at the cost of equity to the twelve-month target, while both multiples apply a benchmark to the last audited year, so the cross-checks are trailing against a forward primary and bias the blend down. We keep the trailing convention because it rests on audited numbers a reader can verify, and we state that on FY2026E metrics the same benchmarks would put the target a few per cent higher. The engine has no forward-multiple switch, so rolling the multiples forward is not available; the direction and rough size of the artefact are disclosed instead of left implicit.

challenges.challenge: The bull ignores the two operating facts that most support it. The body-maker segment is used only as a risk ("already down 45.9% in 2025") although S2 p87 shows it at Rp156.8bn of net segment sales in 9M2026, +40.5% on Rp112bn, with gross profit up to Rp21.1bn. And the radiator line is at 42.8% utilisation (834k units on 1.95m capacity, F5/F6) while filters are at 74.9% (82.66m on 110.4m, F2/F3); the bull narrative mentions the radiator capacity but no bull shock uses it, and all three bull shocks are growth +3pp, margin +1.5pp, payout +6pp.
challenges.answer: Both operating facts are now in the bull. The narrative carries the radiator line at 834k of 1.95m units of capacity and the body-maker line up 40.5% in the nine months, and section 5 states explicitly why we do not add a separate volume shock: radiators contributed 489bn of nine-month sales against 2,985bn for filters and 157bn for body maker, so filling the line and holding the recovery moves group growth by a fraction of a point, which the three-point growth shock already carries.

challenges.challenge: There is no capital-return bull. Net cash of Rp1,196bn is 13% of market cap; the FY2026E FCFE yield at Rp1,595 is 11.3%; capex is 3.6% of revenue; the payout is 72% and the company has raised the dividend for 21 straight years (F89) with 47 quarterly payments since 2015 (F90). The bull payout shock is capped at +6pp "because that is the highest the company has actually paid" (FY2024 76%, F17), which rules out by construction the one thing a cash-rich, debt-free company with no growth capex can do — return the surplus.
challenges.answer: Sized the surplus with the model's own cash build: cash rises from 1,173.4 to 2,889.7 by FY2030E against net debt negative throughout, while the model still pays out 72%. Section 5 explains why no separate special dividend is modelled: the valuation discounts cash flows before financing, so distributing the surplus changes the cash/distribution mix but not enterprise value, and the same mechanics mean the cash built after the forecast starts is not capitalised at all, which makes this a conservative element rather than an aggressive one. The bull payout is raised six points to the top of the historical range, which is the one capital-return action the record shows.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen is half done. The report correctly flags inventory (Rp1,610.3bn from Rp1,250.3bn, +28.8% against COGS +5.2%) and the accruals gap (OCF Rp590.6bn against profit Rp958.3bn), but misses the receivables divergence: third-party trade receivables rose to Rp1,304.8bn from Rp1,173.3bn, +11.2%, which is 1.66x revenue growth of 6.74% and breaches the 1.5x trigger in EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS §2. Working capital is the model's fifth-largest cash item (38.5% of revenue in FY2026E) and this is the second of the two documented channels feeding it.
challenges.answer: Added the receivables test. Section 3 now runs the divergence: third-party trade receivables 1,304.8bn against 1,173.3bn a year earlier while revenue grew 6.7%, more than one and a half times revenue growth, which breaches the method card's trigger, with about a quarter of a year of sales outstanding and the filing's statement that there is no significant concentration of credit risk. It is carried into the bear as a working-capital shock: the bear now adds three points to the NWC ratio because if inventory and receivables keep building at once the ratio is too low, not too high. The basis for the base ratio states both channels.

challenges.challenge: The bear's FX mechanism is inverted and never modelled. §5 says a rupiah through 19,000 is what "rais[es] the dollar cost of steel and filter media faster than the 62% dollar revenue offsets it", but a weaker rupiah lowers the dollar cost of any input that is priced or produced in rupiah; the base case itself says the exposure is "naturally hedged at the gross-margin line". FX is not a scenario shock at all (the three bear shocks are growth, margin, payout), so the margin shock has no stated cause other than this inverted mechanism and "competitors discount".
challenges.answer: The inverted mechanism is gone. Section 5 now states the net FX position in the direction the evidence supports: 62% of nine-month revenue is overseas, so revenue is substantially dollar-linked, and the filings do not disclose the currency split of cost of goods sold, so we cannot net the cost side from the accounts and do not model a rupiah shock at all. The currency reaches the bear through the domestic-discounting channel, because a weaker rupiah makes imported competing parts cheaper in rupiah terms, and the bear narrative attributes the margin shock to that channel alone.

The "sweated asset base" is what supports capex of 3.4% of revenue forever and the widening net cash.
challenges.answer: One capex measure is now used in both places: cash-flow purchases plus advances for fixed assets, which puts FY2025 spend above depreciation of 182.3, consistent with the annual report's realised capital expenditure of 205bn. The 'sweated asset base' language is removed and replaced with the correct rationale for the long-run ratio: maintenance-led spend plus the utilisation headroom in radiators, not a shrinking asset base.

missing_bull_case.note: Two upside arguments are absent. (1) The body-maker line is used only as a risk ("down 45.9% in FY2025") although S2 shows it at Rp156.8bn in 9M2026, +40.5% YoY, and the radiator line runs at 42.8% utilisation (834k of 1.95m units, F5/F6) against filters at 74.9% (82.66m of 110.4m, F2/F3). missing_bear_case.note: The bear is not a bear. It values the shares at Rp2,425, which is 52% ABOVE the Rp1,595 price, so no scenario in the pack produces a loss and the report never explains why the market pays 4.6x EBITDA and 8.2x earnings for this business. Also missing: the receivables divergence (third-party trade receivables to Rp1,304.8bn from Rp1,173.3bn, +11.2%, is 1.66x the +6.74% revenue growth and breaches the 1.5x trigger in EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS §2 — the report flags inventory but not receivables), any check of pledged controlling shares, and the 62%-overseas export book in a 2026 tariff environment.

assumption_realism.note: The revenue build is genuinely bottom-up (9M actual + Q4 at a sourced run-rate) and the tax, minority, payout and NWC inputs all tie to the filings. Three drivers do not. Gross margin is held at 37.43% and the basis claims that is "inside the 35.8-37.1% band the last three periods held" — it is not: FY2023A 35.96%, FY2024A 37.06%, FY2025A 37.05%, 9M2026 36.65%, so 37.43% is 0.37pp above the band top and 0.78pp above the latest actual. And §3 says capex runs "well below depreciation of 182.3" when the pack's own capex basis puts FY2025 at 205.5 (136.0 cash-flow plus 69.0 advances), above D&A.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checked five load-bearing items in the archived sources and all verify verbatim: S2 p6 revenue Rp4,182,808 / gross profit Rp1,533,112 / selling Rp286,140 / G&A Rp162,754 / other operating income Rp147,320 / other operating expenses Rp(59,225) — which reconstructs the 8.63% opex exactly; S5 p13 the FY2025 P&L including other operating income Rp84,006 and expenses Rp(18,132) (so the model's Rp475.95bn opex is right even though the basis note omits the expense line); S3 p662 total depreciation Rp182,262; S4 p3 PT Adrindo 2,910,392,136 shares / 50.54% and "approximately 85% of our revenue is recurring aftermarket revenue"; S4 p18 the 2025 dividend Rp806.21bn / Rp1,125bn / 72% and the 45%-above-Rp30bn policy; S3 p58 auditor Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan (PwC member). Failures remain: the reverse DCF is misquoted three different ways (see C3); §6 asserts the company "is not on the exchange's special monitoring list" with no citation at all; and the rupiah path is attributed to [S0] Yahoo rather than the house deck.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary at 50% with P/E and EV/EBITDA cross-checks is the correct method set for AUTOS_COMPONENTS and the COE build (rf 7.45% + 4.23% ERP + 2.46% CRP, beta 0.91 -> 11.93%, WACC 11.85%) sits inside the house 11-13% band and reconstructs. The bridge is right in sign and size (net cash 1,195.8 added, minorities 519.1 and associates 48.4 netted, all tied to the 30 June pack). But the VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY output contract is not met: no multiple-survival test (the terminal value is 49.4% of the DCF and implies an exit of 8.87x EV/EBITDA on FY2035E against 4.64x entry and 7.36x own four-year average), no statement of terminal ROIC or of the fade that a no-fade perpetuity at 4% g embeds, and no decomposition of the price into implied growth (-7.3%) versus implied return (reproducing Rp1,595 at 4% growth needs a WACC of about 21.5%).

What the prose does not earn is "the market is not necessarily wrong... but the size of the discount implied here is larger than the governance facts support" — a 82.5% expected return needs the discount mechanism named, not asserted, and 55% of the fundamental value rests on the single DCF method.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The AUTOS_COMPONENTS registry is followed correctly (revenue_mode growth, no cost link, the basis for both stated) and the WACC/g/COE match the house deck and band. The deck in this packet carries spot 18,103 and FY2027E 18,350, so the starting point is 533 rupiah too strong, 17,570 -> 19,000 is 8.1% not "roughly a tenth", and the path is cited to [S0] Yahoo rather than to the deck. conservatism_audit.note: Four items sit below the last actual or the level the pack justifies, and two of them are above it. Below: (1) the EV/EBITDA cross-check (20% weight) is run on the pack's LTM EBITDA of 1,544.8, which is the pack's understated-depreciation figure the report itself restates to 1,684.5 in the D&A input — on the restated number the method gives Rp1,855 not Rp1,712 (+8.3%); (2) both cross-checks (50% of the blend) use FY2025A trailing metrics against a forward DCF — on FY2026E metrics the blend is Rp2,682 and the target Rp2,851, not Rp2,760 (+3.3%); (3) Q4 2026E revenue is grossed at 1.02 rather than the FY2025 1.042 seasonal (Rp1,564 vs Rp1,598); (4) Q4 2026E gross margin is 39.5% against the FY2025 Q4 actual of 40.62%. Each item is small; together they roughly net out, but (1) and (2) are documented method inconsistencies, not judgments.

FY2026E revenue of 5,747.2 is 9M2026 actual of 4,182.8 plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate (Q4 1,564.4 vs Q4 2025 1,420.0, +10.2% against Q3's +12.5%) [S2, S4]; the Q4 gross margin of 39.5% is BELOW the 40.62% the FY2025 Q4 earned (FY2025 gross 1,978.1 less 9M2025 1,401.3 on Q4 revenue 1,420.0) [S5, S2]; opex is held flat at the FY2025A 9.1% with no easing [S5]; payout is the observed 72%, not the 45% policy floor [S3, S4]; tax 20.0% matches the 19.79% paid in 9M2026 [S2]. The one asymmetric shock (bear payout -12pp to 60%, bull +6pp to 78%) is justified and points bearish, so the pack is if anything conservative. No unsourced optimism found: every drift away from the last actual is sourced.

findings.finding: The §4 cost-of-capital build does not reconstruct the rate the model uses. The prose states rf 7.45%, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46% and a levered beta of 0.912, which sums to 13.76%, but the engine strikes COE at 11.93% because it first deducts a 1.62% default spread (7.45 - 1.62 = 5.83; 5.83 + 0.912 x 6.69 = 11.93). A reader who redoes the arithmetic from the published inputs gets a rate 1.8pp too high. The rate itself is right and inside the 11-13% house band, so this is a disclosure defect, not a valuation error.

The minority-interest deduction is not struck on the later statement, contrary to §4's claim that "every method is struck on the later statement". The bridge deducts 519.1 (the data pack's June figure) and §4 quotes 498.4 (the FY2025A balance-sheet line), while the 30 September 2026 filing shows NCI of 532.8 (S2 p5). The prose number and the bridge number also disagree with each other by 20.7bn.

The DCF carries no fade of excess returns: terminal-year ROE is 22.4% against a COE of 11.9%, a 10.5pp excess return persisting in perpetuity, and the terminal value is 49.3% of the DCF at 50% weight. VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY §3 allows a no-fade DCF only where the moat mechanism is named AND there is evidence it is widening; §4 names the mechanism but its own evidence is that the moat is "holding rather than widening" (filter line +1.4% against group revenue +6.7% in 9M2026) [S4]. The growth path fades to 4.0% and the margin reverts, but the return on capital does not.

§1 quotes filter capacity of 115.2m pcs (the 9M2026 IR deck, F51) while the FY2025 annual report states 110.4m (F3); utilisation is therefore 71.8% on the newer figure against the 74.9% the red team computed, and "roughly three quarters" sits between the two. Harmless, but the two capacity facts should be reconciled or dated.

flags.message: a.payout: bear -0.12 vs bull 0.06 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The payout shock is deliberately not mirrored. The bear takes the payout to 60%, between the observed 72% and the 45% policy floor the annual report states for net income above Rp 30bn, because the dividend is the first thing a cash squeeze touches [S3]. The bull adds only 6pp to 78%, the FY2024 cash payout ratio of 76% rounded up, because that is the highest the company has actually paid and a payout cannot exceed the earnings it is paid from [S3, S4]. Mirroring to +12pp would put the bull payout at 84%, above any year in the record.

flags.message: expected return +80%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is the sum of three sourced drivers, not a house tilt, and the blend already discounts the DCF by a third. (1) Revenue: the nine months to September 2026 delivered Rp 4,182.8bn, +6.74%, with the third quarter alone up 12.5%, and FY2026E of about Rp 5,747bn is that actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, not a growth assumption [S2, S4]. (2) Margin: the nine-month gross margin of 36.65% (Rp 1,533.1bn on Rp 4,182.8bn) is carried with the fourth quarter at 39.5%, below the 40.62% the FY2025 fourth quarter earned, giving 37.43% for the year against 37.05% in FY2025A, and FY2027E onward reverts to the FY2025A 37.05% [S2, S5]. (3) Cash: the balance sheet is in net cash of about Rp 914bn at 30 September 2026 after the bridge adjustment, and 72% of nine-month profit is already paid or declared as dividends, including the Rp 45 per share third interim [S2, S4, S7]. The reverse DCF on the same 11.85% cost of capital is applied from FY2027E, not to every year: FY2026E stays at our +7.65%, FY2027E solves to -6.33%, and the path then steps down with our own tapering growth to -7.33%, -7.83% and -8.33% by FY2030E, a permanent contraction the nine-month actuals contradict [S0, S2]. The PE and EV/EBITDA cross-checks sit 34% and 42% below the DCF and carry 50% of the weight, so the target is not a single-method artefact.
